name: Rosemaling
basis: why: built from C-scroll, S-scroll, petal and leaf strokes with a two-colour loaded brush; how: motifs by brightness, light-to-dark stroke shading

lumenary.blurb: Rose painting, the folk art of Norway. Scrolls, leaves and flowers are painted with loaded brushes onto a dark ground. Where your picture is bright the flowers bloom, and in the shadows only the scrolls and leaves remain.

facts.bestOn: Warm pictures with bright and dark contrast

why: Rosemaling, rose painting, grew up in Norwegian valleys where country painters decorated chests, bowls and walls in imitation of the grander baroque and rococo styles of the towns. It is built from only a few brush strokes: the C-scroll, the S-scroll, the teardrop petal and the leaf. The painter loads the brush with two colours so every stroke has a light edge and a dark one.
how: Lay motifs on a staggered grid of spacing g.
Choose the motif from the picture’s brightness v: a flower where v is above 0.62, a pair of scrolls from 0.32 to 0.62, and a spray of three leaves below that.
Make the size follow brightness too: R = g (0.3 + 0.34 v).
Pick the nearest of six folk paints (red, ochre, green, blue, cream and brick) to the picture’s colour, or use the picture’s own colours.
Shade every stroke from a light edge to a dark edge, on a teal, black, green or cream ground.
history: The painted style spread across valleys such as Telemark, Hallingdal and Gudbrandsdalen, each with its own manner, and flourished from around the middle of the eighteenth century. After a decline it was revived in Norway, and Norwegian immigrants carried it to the American Midwest, where Per Lysne and others kept it alive at places such as Vesterheim in Iowa.
uses: Folk art decoration and craft classes
terms: Norwegian decorative painting with scrolls, flowers and leaves.
A brush stroke shaped like the letter C.
A region of Norway known for a graceful style of rosemaling.
paragraphs: Rosemaling, “rose painting”, grew up in the valleys of Norway in the eighteenth century, where country painters decorated chests, bowls and walls in imitation of the grander baroque and rococo styles of the towns. It is built from a few brush strokes (the C-scroll, the S-scroll, the teardrop petal, the leaf), and the painter loads the brush with two colours so that every stroke has a light edge and a dark one. The program lays motifs on a staggered grid of spacing g and decides which motif by the brightness v of your picture there: a flower where v is above 0.62, a pair of scrolls from 0.32 to 0.62, and a spray of three leaves below that.

Size follows brightness too: R = g (0.3 + 0.34 v). The colour is the nearest of six folk paints (red, ochre, green, blue, cream and brick) to the picture’s colour, and each paint has a partner for the flower’s centre. Scrolls are tapering ribbons that spiral inward, drawn in pairs turning opposite ways, flowers have petals that are ellipses laid around the centre with a pale highlight, and every shape has a thin dark outline. Scrolls are drawn first, then leaves, then flowers, smallest first, so the largest blossoms sit on top.

equations.note: Motif choice and size (each size is also multiplied by a random 0.92 to 1.08). Places with v below 0.07 (1.4 − d), where d is the density slider, are left bare.
A scroll: a spiral inward over 1.35 turns, drawn as a ribbon that tapers from thick to thin.
The directions of the n petals of a flower, starting from the top.
